title: 10  Signed Measures, Jordan–Hahn Decomposition, and Mutual Singularity
text:
So far, we have discussed nonnegative measures. But can we also introduce a well-defined concept of a signed measure? Indeed we can.






NoteDefinition 10.1 — A signed measure



If \((X, \mathcal M)\) is a measurable space, a signed measure is a map \(\nu: \mathcal M \rightarrow [-\infty, \infty]\) satisfying (i) \(\nu(\emptyset) = 0\) (ii) At most one of the values \(\pm \infty\) are assumed. (iii) If \(A_1, A_2,...\) pairwise disjoint elements of \(\mathcal M\), then \[\nu(\bigcup_i A_i) = \sum_i \nu(A_i)\] where the sum on the RHS converges absolutely when the LHS is finite.


We compare this to the definition of a measure. First, note the additional criterion (ii), and the additional comment in (iii) that the RHS converges absolutely when the LHS is finite. The reason is related to what we discussed earlier, namely that there is no intrinsic ordering of the elements of the set, and consequently, neither should the measure of the union depend on that ordering. Absolute convergence is thus required.
For unsigned series, conditional convergence is not possible, so either the series is absolutely convergent or diverges to \(+\infty\). For signed measures, we can have conditional convergence. Therefore whenever the LHS is finite, we require the RHS to converge absolutely: the union \(\bigcup_i A_i\) does not depend on the order in which we list the \(A_i\), but the value of a conditionally convergent series does, as the side topic below shows.

Side topic: The Riemann rearrangement theorem
The Riemann rearrangement theorem says that if a real series \(\sum_n a_n\) converges but not absolutely, then for every \(L \in [-\infty, \infty]\) there is a rearrangement \(\sigma\) of \(\mathbb N\) such that \[\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{\sigma(n)} = L.\] One can even choose \(\sigma\) so that the partial sums oscillate and approach no limit at all, finite or infinite.
The idea of the proof is simple. Since the series converges conditionally, \(a_n \to 0\), while the positive terms alone sum to \(+\infty\) and the negative terms alone sum to \(-\infty\). To reach a finite \(L\), take positive terms until the partial sum first exceeds \(L\), then negative terms until it first drops below \(L\), then positive terms again, and so on. Every term is eventually used, and since \(a_n \to 0\) the overshoots shrink, so the partial sums converge to \(L\).
A concrete example is the alternating harmonic series, \[1 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac14 + \tfrac15 - \cdots = \ln 2.\] Taking one positive term followed by two negative terms gives \[\Big(1 - \tfrac12\Big) - \tfrac14 + \Big(\tfrac13 - \tfrac16\Big) - \tfrac18 + \cdots = \tfrac12 - \tfrac14 + \tfrac16 - \tfrac18 + \cdots = \tfrac12 \ln 2,\] the same terms with half the sum.
Absolutely convergent series behave well: every rearrangement converges to the same value. This is why condition (iii) of Definition 10.1 asks for absolute convergence. If \(\nu(A_i) = a_i\) for disjoint sets \(A_i\), relabelling the sets does not change their union, so it must not change \(\sum_i \nu(A_i)\) either.

Some remarks that follow from the definition:

A measure is a signed measure.
If \(\mu_1, \mu_2\) are finite measures (or at least one is finite) then \(\mu_1-\mu_2\) is a signed measure.
Condition (ii) is there to avoid having \(\infty - \infty\). For example if \(A, B\) are disjoint sets where \(\nu(A) = \infty\) and \(\nu(B) = -\infty\) then \(\nu(A \bigcup B)\) is undefined.

So far, a signed measure can feel somewhat uncomfortable, especially if we have made ourselves comfortable with the idea that a measure is something that assigns volumes to sets. However, it differences of measures turn out to be very common, and a difference of (finite) measures produces a signed measure, as shown below.






TipRemark 10.2



If \(\mu_1, \mu_2\) are finite measures (or at least one is finite), then the difference \(\mu_1-\mu_2\) is a signed measure.






NoteProof





Properties (i) and (ii) are clearly satisfied. Let \(\Delta \mu := \mu_1 - \mu_2\), then we have \[\Delta \mu (\bigcup_i A_i) = \mu_1(\bigcup_i A_i) - \mu_2(\bigcup_i A_i) = \sum_i \mu_1(A_i) - \sum_i \mu_2(A_i) = \sum_i (\mu_1 - \mu_2)(A_i) = \sum_i \Delta \mu(A_i)\] where subtracting the series is only possible if at least one of them is finite (ok by assumption). Finally, when the LHS is finite, and at least one of measures is finite (say \(\mu_1\)) we have \(\sum_i \mu_1(A_i) < \infty\) since \(A_i\subseteq X\) are disjoint and thus \[\sum_i |\Delta \mu(A_i) |\leq \sum_i \mu_1(A_i) + \sum_i \mu_2(A_i) < \infty\] and thus it converges absolutely. \(\square\)





It turns out that every signed measure has the form \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\), both being measures with at least one being finite. This is the Jordan Decomposition Theorem. Before that, we first prove the Hahn Decomposition Theorem.






NoteDefinition 10.3 — A positive and negative set



If \(\nu\) is a signed measure on \((X,\mathcal M)\), a set \(A \in \mathcal M\) is called a positive set if \(\nu(B) \geq 0\) \(\forall B \subseteq A\) with \(B\in \mathcal M\). A is called a negative set (a null set) if \(\nu(B) \leq (=) 0\) \(\forall B \subseteq A\) with \(B\in \mathcal M\).








ImportantTheorem 10.4 — Hahn Decomposition Theorem



If \(\nu\) is a signed measure on \((X, \mathcal M)\) then \(X\) can be partitioned into two sets \(P, N \in \mathcal M\) (meaning \(P \cup N = X, P \cap N = \emptyset\)) with \(P\) being a positive set and \(N\) a negative set. There is “almost uniqueness” in that if \((P', N')\) is another such partition, then \(P \Delta P'\) and \(N\Delta N'\) are each null sets.








Figure 10.1: Hahn decomposition for \(\nu(A)=\int_A(2x-1)dx\): \(\nu\ge 0\) on \(P\) and \(\nu\le 0\) on \(N\).



By definition we have \(A \Delta B = (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A)\) which are the points which belong to exactly one of the two sets \(A\) and \(B\). In other words, given a signed measure space, we can cleanly partition our \(X\) into a positive and negative measurable part, and this decomposition is unique up to nullsets.






ImportantLemma 10.5 — Existence of positive subset



Let \(\nu\) be a signed measure on \((X, \mathcal M, \nu)\) which does not take the value \(\infty\). If \(\nu(A) > 0\), then there exists a measurable \(B \subseteq A\) where \(\nu(B) > 0\) and \(B\) is a positive set.








CautionExample 10.6



Take \(X = \{1,2,3\}\) and \(\mathcal M = 2^X\) then take \(\nu(\{1\}) = 3\) and \(\nu(\{2\}) = -1\) and same for \(3\). Then \(\nu(X) = 1>0\) but \(\{2\}\subseteq X\) and \(\nu(\{2\}) = -1\), thus \(X\) is not a positive set, although it has positive measure. But if we take \(B = \{1\}\) then indeed we have a subset which is also a positive set. From this perspective it makes sense, the positive and negative parts of \(A\) may give a positive contribution, but we can find a subset of these which only contribute positively. We can do this using a greedy algorithm, by just at each stage remove the most negative measurable subsets, define that as our new subset, remove the negative measurable subsets, and repeat until the resulting subset is positive.








CautionExample 10.7



Take \(([0,1], \mathcal B_{[0,1]})\) with \(\nu(A) = \int_A (2x-1) dm(x)\). If we take \(A = [1/4, 1]\) then \(\nu(A) > 0\) but it is not a positive set since the density \(2x-1 < 0\) on \([1/4, 1/2)\), so why just not remove that interval and define \(B = [1/2,1]\subseteq A\) which is measurable and also a positive set.


This is different from the two facts we mentioned earlier. The lemma says that we only know that the measure of \(A\) is positive, not that it is a positive set. However, it does guarantee that we can always find a subset of \(A\) which is positive.






NoteDefinition 10.8 — Mutually singular measures



Two measures \(\mu, \nu\) on a measurable space \((X, \mathcal M)\) are mutually singular if \(X\) can be partitioned into two disjoint sets \(E, F\) in \(\mathcal M\) so that \(\mu(E) = 0 = \nu(F)\). This is denoted by \(\mu \perp \nu\).








ImportantTheorem 10.9 — (Jordan decomposition theorem)



If \(\nu\) is a signed measure on \((X, \mathcal M)\), then there exists unique measures \(\nu^+\) and \(\nu^-\) so that \(\nu^+ \perp \nu^-\) and \[\nu = \nu^+ - \nu^-\]


The measure \(\nu^+ + \nu^-\) is called the total variation of \(\nu\) and is denoted by \(|\nu|\). The Jordan decomposition theorem is essentially a corollary of the Hahn decomposition theorem where we define \(\nu^\pm\) as the restriction of \(\nu\) to \(P\) (+) \(N\) (-) respectively. This is similiar to the decomposition of a function \[f(x) = \max(f(x), 0) - \max(-f(x), 0) \equiv f^+(x) - f^-(x)\]






CautionExample 10.10



Why is \(\nu(A) = \int_A (2x-1) dx\) a signed measure?

\(\nu(\emptyset) = 0\)
Since \(2x-1\) is bounded on \([0,1]\), it is a finite signed measure and thus never takes \(\pm \infty\).
Countable additivity follows from the fact that the integral and infinite sum can be interchanged by the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem. \[\nu(\bigcup_i A_i) = \int f 1_A dx = \int \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} f \cdot 1_{\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i}\] and in order to swap limit and integral, we need the LDCT. Since \(g_n \rightarrow f \cdot 1_A\) pw and \(|f_n| \leq |f|\) for all n we can simply take \(f\) as our majorant function, and clearly \(\int |f| dx < \infty\) so \(f\) is also integrable. We may therefore write \[=\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \int f_n dx = \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \int_{A_i} f dx = \sum_{i=1}^\infty \nu(A_i)\]









CautionExample 10.11 — Cantor measure minus Lebesgue



Define \[\nu = \mu_c - m\]on the measurable space \(([0,1], \mathcal B_{[0,1]})\) then the Hahn decomposition is simply \(P = C\) (the Cantor set) and \(N= C^c\) and then we simply have \(\nu^+(A) = \mu_c(A \cap C)\) and \(\nu^{-1}(A) = m(A \cap C^c)\) for the Jordan decomposition.

title: 11  Absolute Continuity, Radon–Nikodym Theorem, and Lebesgue Decomposition
text:
NoteDefinition 11.1 — Absolute continuity



Given two measures \(\nu, \mu\) on \((X, \mathcal M)\) we say that \(\nu\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(\mu\), written \(\nu << \mu\), if for all \(A \in \mathcal M\) \[\mu(A) = 0\] implies \(\nu(A) = 0\).




Note that it does not mean that \(\nu \leq \mu\) or vice versa. For example if we have \(\mu\) is the Lebesgue measure on \([0,1]\) and \(\nu\) is two times the Lebesgue measure on the same interval, we have both \(\nu << \mu\) and \(\mu << \nu\).






CautionExample 11.2 — Measures given by a density



Consider a measure space \((X, \mathcal M, \mu)\) and a function \(f\in L^+((X, \mathcal M, \mu))\) then take \[\nu(A) := \int_A f(x) d\mu(x) \tag{1}\] Proving that it is a measure can be done by defining \(g_n : = f 1_{\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i}\) which forms an increasing sequence of measurable functions that converge to \(f \cdot 1_{\bigcup_i A_i}\) pw which allows us to apply the MCT \[\nu\left(\bigcup_i A_i\right) = \int f \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\bigcup_i A_i} \, d\mu = \int \lim_{n\to\infty} g_n \, d\mu \underbrace{=}_{\text{MCT}} \lim_{n\to\infty} \int g_n \, d\mu = \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \int_{A_i} f \, d\mu = \sum_{i=1}^\infty \nu(A_i)\] If \(\mu(A) = 0\), then \(\nu(A) = \int_A f d\mu = 0\) and thus \(\nu << \mu\).


The measure \(\nu\) in (1) is often denoted simply by \(f\mu\). In fact, any measure which is absolutely continuous with respect to \(\mu\) has this form assuming \(\sigma\)-finiteness.






ImportantTheorem 11.3 — The Radon-Nikodym theorem



Let \(\nu, \mu\) be two measures on \((X, \mathcal M)\) with \(\nu << \mu\) and with \(\nu, \mu\) being \(\sigma\)-finite. Then, there exists a measurable function \(f_0: X \rightarrow [0,\infty)\) such that \(\forall A \in \mathcal M\) we have \[\nu(A) = \int_A f_0(x) d\mu(x)\] Morever, \(f_0\) is unique in the sense that if \(g_0\) is another such function, then \[\mu(\{x:f_0(x) \neq g_0(x)\})=0\]In other words \(\mu\) is defined up to a \(\mu\)-null set. Thus any two \(f_0, g_0\) agree \(\mu\)-a.e.






NoteProof





We prove this under the assumption that \(\mu, \nu\) are finite, and only outline the extension to the \(\sigma\)-finite case. First define \[\mathcal F := \{f: X \rightarrow [0, \infty):\int_A f(x) d\mu(x) \leq \nu(A) \forall A \in \mathcal M\}\] Note that \(\mathcal F\) is nonempty since \(f \equiv 0\) is in \(\mathcal F\). Therefore, the supremum is defined, and we let \[m:=\sup \{ \int f(x) d\mu(x) : f\in \mathcal F\}\]where \(m\leq \nu(X) < \infty\).
Claim: There exists \(f_0 \in \mathcal F\) for which \(\int f_0(x) d\mu(x) = m\), i.e. the supremum is achieved.
Note that if \(h_1, h_2 \in \mathcal F\), then so does \(\max\{h_1, h_2\}\), since \[\int_A \max\{h_1, h_2\} d\mu(x) = \int_{A \cap \{h_1 \geq h_2\}} h_1(x) d\mu(x) + \int_{A \cap \{h_1 < h_2\}} h_2(x) d\mu(x) \leq \nu(A \cap \{h_1 \geq h_2\}) + \nu(A \cap \{h_1 > h_2\}) = \nu(A)\]Now we choose \(h_1, h_2, ... \in \mathcal F\) so that \[\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \int h_n(x) d\mu(x) = m \tag{2}\]Why can we do this? Well, by the definition of the supremum, for every \(\epsilon > 0\) there exists some \(f\in \mathcal F\) with \(\int f d\mu > m -\epsilon\), we may thus take \(\epsilon = 1/n\) to construct our sequence \(h_n \in \mathcal F\).
If we let \(g_n:= \max\{h_1,...,h_n\}\), then each \(g_n \in \mathcal F\) (by induction) and \(g_n\) is increasing and \[\int h_n(x) d\mu(x) \leq \int g_n d\mu \leq m\] where the left inequality holds since \(g_n \geq h_n\) by definition. The right inequality holds because \(g_n \in \mathcal F\) and thus \(\int g_n d\mu \leq m\) by definition of m. By the squeeze theorem of (2), we thus have
\[\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \int g_n d\mu  = m\]
If we can move \(\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}\) inside the integral, we have found our \(f_0\). In particular, by setting \(f_0 := \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} g_n\). Are we allowed to make this exchange of limiting operations? Well clearly the \(g_n\)’s form a sequence of nonnegative increasing measurable functions (being the maximum of elements in \(\mathcal F\)) which allows us to apply MCT \[\int f_0(x) d\mu(x) = m\]What remains to show for the claim is that \(f_0 \in \mathcal F\). For this, fix \(A \in \mathcal A\). We want to apply MCT to \(g_n 1_A\) whose limit is given by \(f_0 1_A\) and thus we have \[\int_A f_0 d\mu =  \int f_0 1_A d\mu = \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \int g_n 1_A d\mu = \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \int_A g_n d\mu\] but since every \(g_n \in \mathcal F\), for every \(n\) we have \[\int_A g_n d\mu \leq \nu(A)\] and thus taking the limit we still have \[\int_A f_0 d\mu = \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \int_A g_n d\mu \leq \nu(A)\]Which proves the claim.
Now we define \[\nu_0 := \nu - f_0 \mu\]and our goal is to show that it is the zero measure, meaning that \(\nu_0(A) = 0 \forall A \in \mathcal M\). Note that by construction of \(f_0\), we have \(\nu_0(A) \geq 0\).
By showing \(\nu_0(X) = 0\) is true, and using the fact that \(\nu_0\) is a positive measure by construction, we have \(\nu_0(A) = 0 \forall A \in \mathcal M\). Thus, from now on, assume for sake of contradiction that \(\nu_0(X) > 0\). This is just a finite number, and since \(\mu\) is finite by assumption, there exists an \(\epsilon > 0\) so that \[\nu_0(X) - \epsilon \mu(X) > 0 \tag{3}\] Now let \((P,N)\) be the Hahn decomposition for the signed measure \[\nu_0 - \epsilon \mu\]which is just the difference of two positive measures. This construction always exists, so far so good!
When constructing the Hahn decomposition, we either have \(\mu(P) = 0\) or \(\mu(P) > 0\), since \(\mu\) is a measure. We will see that both cases leads to a contradiction, assuming \(\nu_0(X) > 0\) (or equivalently statement (3)).
Case 1: \(\mu(P) = 0\), then since \(\nu << \mu\) we have that \(\nu(P) = 0\) and hence \((\nu_0 - \epsilon \mu)(P) = (\nu - f_0 \mu - \epsilon \mu)(P) = 0\), contradicting (3) since \[(\nu_0 - \epsilon \mu)(X) = (\nu_0 - \epsilon \mu)(P) + (\nu_0 - \epsilon \mu)(N) = (\nu_0 - \epsilon \mu)(N)\]but by the Hahn decomposition that is \(\leq 0\) and not \(>0\).
Case 2: \(\mu(P) > 0\). Note that \[g_0 = f_0 + \epsilon 1_P \in \mathcal F\]As follows from\[\int_A (f_0 + \epsilon 1_p) d\mu(x) = \int_A f_0 d\mu(x) + \epsilon \mu(P \cap A) \leq \int_A f_0 d\mu(x) + \nu_0(P \cap A) \leq \int_A f_0 d\mu(x) + \nu_0(A) = \nu(A)\] where we used that \(\nu_0(P \cap A) \geq \epsilon \mu(P\cap A)\) since \(P \cap A \subseteq P\) is a positive subset and similarly \(\nu_0(P \cap A) \leq \nu_0(A)\) by monotonicity (with \(\nu_0\) being a positive measure).
Next, since \(\mu(P) > 0\) we have \[\int g_0 d\mu(x) = m + \epsilon \mu(P) > m\]contradicting the definition of \(m\), since \(g_0 \in \mathcal F\). Hence \(\nu_0\) is the zero measure.
Outline for the \(\sigma\)-finite extension:

Break up \(X\) into countably many pieces, each piece with finite \(\mu, \nu\) measure. Then one can do the above on each piece separately and put it together in the end. \(\square\)












Figure 11.1: The Radon–Nikodym derivative is the density whose area over \(A\) is \(\nu(A)\).









TipRemark 11.4 — About the Radon–Nikodym theorem




We call \(f_0\) in the above theorem for the Radon-Nikodym derivative of \(\nu\) with respect to \(\mu\).
If \(\mu\) is Lebesgue measure on \((R, \mathcal B)\) and \(\nu\) is the distribution of a random variable which is absolutely continuous with respect to \(\mu\), then \(f_0\) is simply the probability density function from elementary probability.
The theorem is false in general without the \(\sigma\)-finite assumption on \(\mu\).
It turns out that \(\sigma\)-finiteness on \(\nu\) is not needed provided that \(f_0\) is allowed to take the value \(\infty\).



Note that every random variable \(X\) has a cumulative distribution function (CDF), defined from its distribution \(\mu_X\) (Definition 9.4) by \[F_X(x) = \mu_X\big((-\infty, x]\big) = P\big(X^{-1}((-\infty, x])\big).\] By Proposition 4.3 it is weakly increasing and right continuous. A probability density function (PDF), on the other hand, only exists when \(\mu_X\) is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure (Definition 11.1), and it is then the Radon–Nikodym derivative \(d\mu_X/dm\) (see the remarks after Theorem 11.3).
Conversely, given a function \(F\) with these properties, Proposition 4.4 gives a unique finite Borel measure \(\mu_F\) whose CDF is \(F\), and from \(\mu_F\) we can construct a random variable whose law is \(\mu_F\). Since \(\mu_F\) is finite it is \(\sigma\)-finite, but it need not be absolutely continuous, so it need not have a PDF. The Cantor measure \(\mu_C\) (Theorem 4.8) is an example: its CDF is the Cantor function, but \(\mu_C\) is singular, so it has no density.






CautionExample 11.5 — Sampling from a distribution via its CDF



The fact that every CDF comes with a random variable is also useful in practice, for simulating random variables with a given distribution. Generate \(U \sim \mathcal U(0,1)\) and set \(X = F_X^{-1}(U)\). When \(F_X\) is continuous and strictly increasing, \[P(X \le x) = P\big(U \le F_X(x)\big) = F_X(x),\] so \(X\) has the CDF \(F_X\). This requires being able to evaluate \(F_X^{-1}\), which is not always easy (see simulation via the CDF).
For example, one way to generate a normal \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) random variable is to start from \(U \sim \mathcal U(0,1)\), set \(Z = \Phi^{-1}(U)\), which has the standard normal distribution, and finally let \(X = \sigma Z + \mu\). Here \(\Phi^{-1}\) has no closed form, but it is easy to evaluate numerically.



Side topic: The Kullback–Leibler divergence
Radon–Nikodym derivatives give a natural way to compare two probability distributions. Let \((\Omega, \mathcal T)\) be a measurable space and let \(\mu, \nu\) be probability measures on it with \(\mu \ll \nu\). The Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of \(\mu\) from \(\nu\) is
\[KL(\mu \,\|\, \nu) = \int \log\frac{d\mu}{d\nu}\, d\mu,\]
where \(\frac{d\mu}{d\nu}\) is the Radon–Nikodym derivative of \(\mu\) with respect to \(\nu\) (Theorem 11.3). If \(\mu \not\ll \nu\), the KL divergence is set to \(+\infty\) by convention.
What it measures. The KL divergence measures how different \(\mu\) is from the reference distribution \(\nu\), so it plays the role of a distance between two distributions. The integrand \(\log\frac{d\mu}{d\nu}\) compares, point by point, how much mass \(\mu\) puts somewhere relative to \(\nu\), and the integral averages this log-ratio over \(\mu\). It is always nonnegative and equals \(0\) exactly when \(\mu = \nu\). In information theory, \(KL(\mu \,\|\, \nu)\) is the expected extra information needed to describe samples from \(\mu\) when using a code designed for \(\nu\).
The familiar formula with densities. Suppose both \(\mu, \nu \ll m\), with \(m\) the Lebesgue measure. By the Radon–Nikodym theorem they have densities \(p = \frac{d\mu}{dm}\) and \(q = \frac{d\nu}{dm}\), and these are exactly the probability density functions from elementary probability (see the remarks after Theorem 11.3). Then \(\frac{d\mu}{d\nu} = \frac{p}{q}\) where \(q > 0\), and \(d\mu = p\,dm\), so substituting gives
\[KL(\mu \,\|\, \nu) = \int p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\, dx.\]
The KL divergence is also the standard training objective for normalizing flows, where one minimizes the KL divergence between a target distribution and a transformed base distribution; see the review by Papamakarios et al. (2021).








Figure 11.2: Interactive: a one-dimensional normalizing flow \(T_t\) carries the base distribution \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) to a two-bump target. The density \(p_t\) follows from the change of variables formula, and \(KL(p_t \,\|\, \text{target})\) drops to \(0\) at \(t=1\).









ImportantTheorem 11.6 — Lebesgue Decomposition Theorem



Let \(\nu, \mu\) be two measures on \((X, \mathcal M)\), with \(\nu, \mu\) being \(\sigma\)-finite. Then there exists unique measures \(\nu_{ac}, \nu_s\) so that \[\nu = \nu_{ac} + \nu_s\]where \[\nu_{ac} << \mu\] and \[\nu_s \perp \mu\]


The decompositions is relate to the measure \(\mu\). The measure is split into an absolutely continuous part, which can be written as \(f_0 \mu\) for some \(f_0\) by Radon-Nikodyn, and one singular component to which \(\mu\) is “blind to”.
We mention some other important but simple decompositions. Given any \(\sigma\)-finite mesure space \((X, \mathcal M, \mu)\) with single points being measurable, we can decompose \(\mu\) into an atomic peice and continuous piece. If \(\mathcal A\) is the set of atoms, we write \[\mu = \mu\vert_{A} + \mu\vert_{A^c}\]and it is easy to check that these are mutually singular.






ImportantProposition 11.7 — Measure-theoretic analogue of \(\epsilon-\delta\) continuity



Let \(\mu, \nu\) be measures with \(\nu\) finite. Then \(\nu <<  \mu\) iff \(\forall \epsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) so that for all measurable sets \(A\) we have \[\mu(A) < \delta\] implies \[\nu(A) < \epsilon\]






NoteProof





\(\Rightarrow :\) Assume the \(\epsilon-\delta\) condition. Suppose \(\mu(A) = 0\). Fix \(\epsilon > 0\). By the condition, we have that \(\mu(A) < \delta\) implies \(\nu(A) < \epsilon\). Since \(\mu(A) = 0 < \delta\) we have \(\nu(A) < \epsilon\). Since \(\epsilon > 0\) arbitrary and \(\nu(A) \geq 0\) we have \(\nu(A) = 0\). \(\Leftarrow:\) We prove the contrapositive argument. If the \(\epsilon-\delta\) condtion fails, we have \(\nu \not\ll \mu\). If it fails, it means \(\exists \epsilon_0 > 0\) and sets \((A_n)\) with \(\mu(A_n) < 1/2^n\) and \(\nu(A_n) \geq \epsilon_0\). Now consider \(A = \limsup A_n\). Borel Cantelli says that \(\mu(A) = 0\). On the other hand, \(\nu(A) \geq \epsilon_0\) since for every n \(\nu(\bigcup_{k\geq n} A_k) \geq \epsilon_0\) and taking limit as \(n\rightarrow \infty\) and using continuity from above for \(\nu\) (valid since \(\nu\) is finite measure) we have that \(\nu \not \ll \mu\). \(\square\)





This is the measure-theoretic analogue of \(\epsilon-\delta\) continuity, where the role of distance bw points is replaced by \(\mu\) and the distance between function values is played by \(\nu(A)\). So the propositoin \(\nu << \mu\) is equivalent to \(\nu\) being continuous with respect to \(\mu\).

title: 12  The 3× Covering Lemma
text:
We now start a new chapter which will study differentiation in \(\mathbb R^n\).






ImportantTheorem 12.1 — Simple theorem



Let \(f: [0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb R\) be monotone, then for a.e. \(x\), \(f\) is differentiable with a finite derivative.








ImportantTheorem 12.2 — The fundamental theorem of calculus



First fundamental theorem of calculus: if \(f\) is a continous function on \([a,b]\)d \[F(x) = \int_a^x f(t) dt\] then \[F'(x) = x \forall x.\] Second fundamental theorem of calculus: If \(f\) is a continuously differentiable function on \([a,b]\) then \[\int_a^b f'(x) dx = f(b) - f(a)\]


We first discuss the first fundamental theorem, and argue that it cannot possibly hold for all measurable bounded functions. If \(f\) is continuous function and \(g\) any measurable function which agrees with \(f\) a.e., then we have \[\int_a^x f(t) dt = \int_a^x g(t) dt\]for every \(x\), hence for every \(x\) we have \[ \left( \int_a^x g(t) dt\right)'(x) = f(x)\] and therefore \[ \left( \int_a^x g(t) dt\right)'(x) = g(x)\]will fail at every point where \(f(x) \neq g(x)\). However, we do have \[ \left( \int_a^x g(t) dt\right)'(x) = g(x) \ \mathrm{a.e.}\]So the most we can hope for a bounded measurable \(f\) is that the first fundamental theorem holds at a.e. \(x\). We will show this and generalize it to higher dimensions, which we will be called Lebesgue’s differentiation theorem.
Note that continuous functions are also measurable. To see this, take \(U \subseteq \mathbb R\) then \[f^{-1}(U)\]must be open by continuity. And since open sets in \([a,b]\) are Borel sets. Since the Borel algebra is generated by all open sets of the real line, we have that the preimage of any Borel set is also in \(\mathcal B_{[a,b]}\) so \(f\) is measurable. But not every measurable function is continuous.

Approximations by sets and by continuous functions
The Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathbb R^n\), denoted by \(\mathcal B^n\) can be described as generated by open sets in \(\mathbb R^n\) or as the product \(\sigma\)-algebra coming from \((\mathbb R, \mathcal B)\).






ImportantTheorem 12.3




For any Borel set \(E \subseteq \mathbb R^n\) we have \[m(E) = \sup\{ m(K) : K \subseteq E, K \mathrm{compact}\}\]
If \(f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n, \mathcal B^n, m)\) and \(\epsilon > 0\), then there exists a continuous function \(g\) on \(\mathbb R^n\) so that \[\int_{\mathbb R^n} |f(x) - g(x)| dm(x) < \epsilon\]



Theorem 12.3(i) is sometimes referred to as approximation from within by compact sets.
We will also need to approximate sets with respect to other measures.






NoteDefinition 12.4 — Regular



A Borel measure \(\nu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\) is regular if \(\nu(K) < \infty\) for all compact sets \(K \subseteq \mathbb R^n\).


An example of a regular Borel measure is the Lebesgue measure. An example of a non-regular Borel measure is the counting measure.






ImportantTheorem 12.5 — Approximating from outside using open sets



Let \(\nu\) be a regular Borel measure on \(\mathbb R^n\). If \(E\) is a Borel set then \[\nu(E) = \mathrm{inf}\{\nu(O) : E \subseteq O, O \ \mathrm{open}\}\]


Since the Lebesgue measure is also regular, it satisfies both outer regularity and inner regularity, meaning the measure can be approximated from the outside using open sets or from the inside using compact sets.
Since the counting measure is not regular, it fails the above theorem. Take for example \(E = \{0\}\), then \(\nu(E) = 1\). But any open set containing \(0\) contains an interval \((-\epsilon, \epsilon)\), thus \(\nu(O) = \infty\). Note however that for inner regularity, we can simply take \(K = \{0\}\) which is compact (single points are compact), so the supremum is achieved.


A covering lemma






ImportantTheorem 12.6 — A simple covering lemma



Let \(A_1,...,A_k\) be open balls in \(\mathbb R^2\). There is a subset \(B_1,...,B_l\) of these which are disjoint and that satisfy \[\sum_{j=1}^l m(B_j) \geq \frac{m(\bigcup_{i=1}^k A_i)}{9}\]






NoteProof





Let \(B_1\) be the largest of \(A_1,...,A_k\). Remove all remaining \(A_i\)’s which intersect \(B_1\). Let \(B_2\) be the largest of the remaining \(A_i\)’s. Remove all remaining \(A_i\)’s which intersect \(B_2\). Let \(B_3\) be largest of remaining … and continue until no \(A_j\)’s are left. This produces \(B_1, ..., B_l\) which are disjoint by construction. \(\square\)












Figure 12.1: Interactive: the greedy algorithm behind the covering lemma. The chosen balls are disjoint, and their 3× enlargements cover all the balls.



Claim If \(A_i\) is NOT in the final list, then for some \(j\) we have \[A_i \subseteq B_j^\star\] where \(^\star\) denotes the ball concentric with \(B_j\) but three times the radius. Since \(A_i\) was not chosen, it must have intersected one of the \(B_j\)’s. The first \(B_j\) it intersects must be as large as \(A_i\) since otherwise we would have chosen \(A_i\) instead. We must therefore have \[r(A_i) \leq r(B_j)\] and since they intersect, we have \[d(\mathrm{center}(A_i), \mathrm{center}(B_j)) < r(A_i) + r(B_j)\]Thus for any point \(x\in A_i\) we have \[d(x, \mathrm{center}(B_j)) \leq d(x, \mathrm{center}(A_i)) + d(\mathrm{center}(A_i), \mathrm{center}(B_j)) < 2r(A_i) + r(B_j) < 3r(B_j)\] You can think of this as three contributions depending on







Figure 12.2: Interactive: why the factor \(3\) is needed in the covering lemma.



In the case where \(A_i\) was selected, then \(A_i = B_j\) for some j, then \(B_j \subseteq B_j^\star\) trivially. But if it was eliminated, we had that \(A_i \subseteq B_j^\star\), so every \(A_i\) is contained in some \(B_j^\star\), meaning \[\bigcup_i A_i \subseteq \bigcup_j B_j^\star\]
We thus obtain, by applying monotonicity and countable subadditivity \[m(\bigcup_{i=1}^k A_i) \leq m(\bigcup_{j=1}^l B_j^\star) \leq \sum_{j=1}^l m(B_j^\star) = 9 \sum_{j=1}^l m(B_j)\] as desired.






ImportantTheorem 12.7 — A covering lemma



Let \(\mathcal C\) be a collection of open balls in \(\mathbb R^n\) with \(U\) being their union. \(\forall c < m(U)\), there exists \(B_1, B_2,..., B_k \in \mathcal C\) which are disjoint satisfying \[\sum_{i=1}^k m(B_i) \geq \frac{c}{3^n}\]


Before constructing the proof, we notice two differences between this covering lemma and the simpler covering lemma. First of all, there is no assumption about the collection \(\mathcal C\) being finite. The conclusion is about \(c\) and not \(m(U)\) too.
Since \(c < m(U)\), by Theorem 12.3(i) we can choose \(K \subseteq U\) compact s.t. \(m(K) > c\). A compact set has finite subcover, meaning we can take \(A_1,...,A_m \in \mathcal C\) that cover \(K\). Now we repeat the same steps as before, choosing \(B_1\) being among those of maximal size, then choose \(B_2\) among these to have maximal size but disjoint from \(B_1\), and repeating. The claim is identical as before, meaning if \(A_i\) is NOT in the final list, then for some \(j\) we have \[A_i \subseteq B_j^\star\] where \(^\star\) denotes the ball concentric with \(B_j\) but three times the radius. Since \(A_i\) was not chosen, it must have intersected one of the \(B_j\)’s. Unlike before however, the measure is bounded by a factor of \(3^n\) instead. \[c < m(K) < m(\bigcup_{j=1}^k B_j^\star) \leq \sum_{j=1}^k m(B_j^\star) = 3^n \sum_{j=1}^k m(B_j)\] as desired.

title: 13  Hardy–Littlewood Maximal Function and the Maximal Theorem
text:
In what follows, we will denote \(B(x,r)\) the open ball centered at \(x\) with radius \(r\).






NoteDefinition 13.1 — Locally integrable



A function \(f:\mathbb R^n \rightarrow \mathbb R\) is said to be locally integrable, or in \(L_\mathrm{loc}^1\), if \(f\) is integrable with respect to Lebesgue measure when restricted to any compact set. (or equivalently, if for every \(x\) there is an \(r > 0\) such that \(f\) is integrable on \(B(x,r)\) wrt to Lebesgue measure.)


For \(f\in L_\mathrm{loc}^1\), \(x\in \mathbb R^n\), and \(r > 0\) we define \[A_r f(x) = \frac{1}{m(B(x,r))} \int_{B(x,r)} f(y) dm(y)\]which is simply the average of \(f\) over the ball around \(x\) with radius \(r\). This can be seen interpreted as the mean value of \(f\) over the ball centered around \(x\) with radius \(r\).
Some additional remarks:

If \(f\) is continuous at \(x\), it is easy to see that \[\lim_{r\rightarrow 0} A_r f(x) = f(x)\]
This cannot occur for all \(f\) since if we modify it at a single point, it would fail there. Take for example \(\tilde f(x) =1\) but \(\tilde f(y) = 0, y \neq x\), then the limit becomes \(0\) as \(r\rightarrow 0\) whereas the LHS is \(1\).







NoteDefinition 13.2 — Hardy-Littlewood Maximal function



If \(f\in L^1_\mathrm{loc}(\mathbb R^n)\), then the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function \(Hf\) is defined by \[Hf(x) := \sup_{r> 0} A_r|f|(x)\]









Figure 13.1: Interactive: the averages \(A_r|f|(x)\) over the window \([x-r,x+r]\) (red), and the maximal function \(Hf(x) = \sup_{r>0} A_r|f|(x)\) (blue). The right panel plots \(r \mapsto A_r|f|(x)\); its supremum is \(Hf(x)\).



This functions essentially computes the average over the absolute value of \(f\) over all radii, and picks the largest such average amongst those radii. It is therefore a “measure” of the local average of \(|f|\).
One can verify that \(Hf\) is a measurable function by noting \[(Hf)^{-1}(\alpha, \infty) =\bigcup_{r>0} (A_r|f|)^{-1}\{(\alpha, \infty)\}\]where \(A_rf\) is a continuous function for \(f\in L^1_\mathrm{loc}\), and thus we have preimages of open sets under continuous functions which are still open, and thus \((Hf)^{-1}(\alpha, \infty)\) is a union of open sets.






ImportantTheorem 13.3 — (Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Theorem)



If \(f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)\), then \(\forall \alpha > 0\) we have \[m(\{x: Hf(x) > \alpha\}) \leq \frac{3^n}{\alpha} \int |f|dm(x)\]






NoteProof





Let \(E_\alpha = \{x: Hf(x) > \alpha\}\). For each \(x\in E_\alpha\) there exists \(r_x > 0\) so that \[A_{r_x}|f|(x) > \alpha\] by the definition of the supremum. With this, we can for each \(x\) have an associated open ball, and we may denote this collection of open balls as \(\mathcal C\). Given \(c < m(\bigcup_{x\in E_a} B(r, r_x))\), we can use the covering lemma from Lecture 12 to find \(x_1, ..., x_k\) in \(E_\alpha\) so that \(k\) balls \(\{B(x_i, r_{x_i})\}\) are disjoint and \[\frac{c}{3^n} \leq \sum_{i=1}^k m(B(x_i, r_{x_i}))\] However, by our choice of \(r_x\)’s, i.e. \(A_{r_{x_i}}|f|(x_i) > \alpha\), we have \[\frac{c}{3^n} \leq \sum_{i=1}^k m(B(x_i, r_{x_i})) \leq \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{1}{\alpha}\int_{B(x_i, r_{x_i})} |f|(x) dm(x) \leq \frac{1}{\alpha} \int |f|(x) dm(x)\]where the last inequality follows from the disjointness of the balls. Since this holds \(\forall c < m(E_\alpha)\), we also have \[m(E_\alpha) \leq \frac{3^n}{\alpha} \int |f|dm\] as desired. \(\square\)

title: 14  Lebesgue’s Differentiation Theorem
text:
ImportantTheorem 14.1 — The differentiation theorem for functions



If \(f \in L^1_\mathrm{loc}(\mathbb R^n)\) then for Lebesgue a.e. point \(x\) we have \[\lim_{r\rightarrow 0} A_r f(x) = f(x)\]






NoteProof





It suffices to show this a.e. point in \([- N, N]^n\). If it holds for every N, it also holds for the full \(\mathbb R^n\) since countable union of nullset is still a nullset. Therefore we may assume \(f\) is 0 outside of \([-N-1, N+1]^n\) since we are anyways taking the limit as \(r\rightarrow 0\) in the end, in which case we have that \(f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)\). This will be needed when we apply Hardy-Littlewoods maximal theorem. For any \(\alpha >  0\) let \[E_\alpha = \{ x : \limsup_{r\rightarrow 0} |A_rf(x) - f(x)| > \alpha\}\]If we can show that \(m(E_\alpha)  =0\) for each \(\alpha\), then this implies the theorem since the set of points where the conclusion of the theorem fails is equal to \(\bigcup_n E_{1/n}\) which then also has measure zero (which is just the definition of the statement being true a.e.)
It is not obvious a priori that \(E_\alpha\) is Lebesgue measurable, however we will show it is contained inside a measurable sets of arbitrarily small measure, and its outer measure is thus zero and by completeness it will be Lebesgue measurable.
Now fix \(\alpha > 0\) and show \(m(E_\alpha) = 0\). Fix \(\epsilon > 0\). By Theorem 12.3 we can find a continuous integrable function \(g\) such that \[\int_{\mathbb R^n} |f(x) -g(x)| dm(x) < \epsilon\] and thus\(f-g \in L^1(\mathbb R^N\)). Observe that \[\limsup_{r\rightarrow 0}|A_r f(x) - f(x)| \leq \limsup_{r\rightarrow 0}|A_r(f-g)(x)| + \limsup_{r\rightarrow 0}|A_rg(x) - g(x)| + \limsup_{r\rightarrow 0}|g(x) - f(x)|\] by the triangle inequality. The first term is at most \(H(f-g)(x)\), and the second term is zero since the theorem is easily checked for continuous functions. Hence \[\limsup_{r\rightarrow 0}|A_r f(x) - f(x)| \leq H(f-g)(x) + |g(x)-f(x)|\]If the first term is larger than \(\alpha\), then at least one of the terms on the RHS have to be larger than \(\alpha/2\), i.e. \[E_\alpha \subseteq \{x: H(f-g)(x) > \alpha/2\} \cup \{x: |g(x) - f(x)| > \alpha/2\}\] which is the union of two measurable sets, being preimages of measurable functions of Borel sets, and thus the outer measure and Lebesgue measure agree (being measurable) Hence \[m^\star(E_\alpha) \leq m^\star(U) = m(\{x: H(f-g)(x) > \alpha/2\}) +m( \{x: |g(x) - f(x)| > \alpha/2\})\] Using Theorem 13.3 for the first term and Markov’s inequality for the second we obtain \[m(E_\alpha) \leq \frac{2)(3)^n}{\alpha} \epsilon + \frac{2}{\alpha}\epsilon\]And since \(\epsilon > 0\) arbitrary and the outer measure of \(E_\alpha\) is zero, and the measure space is complete, \(E_\alpha\) is also Lebesgue measurable with measure \(m(E_\alpha) = 0\). \(\square\)











Figure 14.1: Left: the averages (dashed) of \(f\) over the shrinking intervals \(B(x,r)\). Right: the averages \(A_rf(x)\) converge to \(f(x)\) as \(r\to0\), which happens at almost every point.



What the above theorem tells us is that for any locally integrable function \(f\), one has for Lebesgue a.e. \(x\): \[\lim_{r\to 0} \frac{1}{m(B(x,r))} \int_{B(x,r)} (f(y) - f(x))\, dm(y) = 0\]
This might be due to some cancellation. The following stronger result shows that this is not the case.






ImportantTheorem 14.2 — Lebesgue points



For any locally integrable function \(f\), one has for Lebesgue a.e. \(x\): \[\lim_{r\to 0} \frac{1}{m(B(x,r))} \int_{B(x,r)} |f(y) - f(x)|\, dm(y) = 0\]
The set of \(x\) where this holds is called the Lebesgue set of \(f\), denoted \(\mathcal{L}_f\).


The Lebesgue points of a function \(f\) are therefore interpreted as points where \(f\) does not oscillate too much, in an average sense. Finally, Theorem 14.2 is a stronger version of Theorem 14.1, and will allow us to replace balls by other types of sets (see Corollary 14.4).






NoteDefinition 14.3 — Shrinks Nicely



A collection of Borel sets \(\{E_r\}_{0<r\leq 1}\) is said to shrink nicely to \(x\) if for all \(r \in (0,1]\):

\(E_r \subseteq B(x,r)\)
There exists \(\alpha > 0\) such that \(m(E_r) \geq \alpha\, m(B(x,r))\) for all \(r\).

The second condition says that each \(E_r\) occupies a substantial proportion of \(B(x,r)\). Note there is no requirement that \(x \in E_r\).








ImportantCorollary 14.4 — Lebesgue Points and Nicely Shrinking Sets



Let \(f\) be locally integrable. If \(x \in \mathcal{L}_f\) (and hence for \(m\)-a.e. \(x\)) and \(\{E_r\}_{0<r\leq 1}\) are Borel sets shrinking nicely to \(x\), then: \[\lim_{r\to 0} \frac{1}{m(E_r)} \int_{E_r} |f(y) - f(x)|\, dm(y) = 0\] and \[\lim_{r\to 0} \frac{1}{m(E_r)} \int_{E_r} f(y)\, dm(y) = f(x)\]


As a special case if \(f\in L^1([0,1])\) and letting \(E_r(x) = [x, x+r]\) one has \[(\int_0^x f(t) dm(t))'(x) =f(x)\] for a.e. x.






ImportantTheorem 14.5 — Differentiation Theorem for Measures



Let \(\nu\) be a regular Borel measure on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) whose Lebesgue decomposition with respect to Lebesgue measure is given by \(\nu = \nu_s + fm\). Then \[\lim_{r\to 0} \frac{\nu(B(x,r))}{m(B(x,r))}\] exists and equals \(f(x)\) for Lebesgue a.e. \(x\).
Remark: If \(\nu \ll m\), this reduces to Theorem 14.1.


The intuition for the above result is that \(\nu_s(N^c) = 0\) and \(m(N)=0\) (by singularity), so \(\nu_s\) puts all its mass on \(N\), which is a Lebesgue null set. Thus, the ratio tells us that if we zoom into the measure \(\nu\) by looking at how much mass it puts in a tiny ball around \(x\), normalized by the volume, we recover the density \(f\) at almost every point.
It turns out we can generalize the above theorem to nicely shrinking sets.






ImportantCorollary 14.6 — Differentiation for Measures over Nicely Shrinking Sets



Let \(\nu\) be a regular Borel measure on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) whose Lebesgue decomposition with respect to Lebesgue measure is given by \(\nu = \nu_s + fm\). Then for Lebesgue a.e. \(x\), if \(\{E_r\}_{0<r\leq 1}\) are Borel sets shrinking nicely to \(x\), then \[\lim_{r\to 0} \frac{\nu(E_r)}{m(E_r)} = f(x)\]








ImportantTheorem 14.7 — Right continuous function has finite derivative



Let \(F\) be a right continuous increasing function on \([0,1]\). Then \(F\) has a finite derivative at Lebesgue a.e. \(x\).

title: 15  Functions of Bounded Variation, Absolute Continuity, and the FTC
text:
NoteDefinition 15.1 — Total variation, bounded variation and unbounded variation



If \(f:[0,1]\rightarrow \mathbb R\) we define the total variation of \(f\) on \([a,b] \subseteq [a,b]\) to be \[TV_{[a,b]}(f) := \sup \{\sum_{i=1}^n |f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1}) \} : a = x_0 < x_1 < x_2 <...<x_n = b\}\] We say \(f\) is of bounded variation on \([a,b]\) if \(TV_{[a,b]}f < \infty\) and of unbounded variation otherwise.








Figure 15.1: The variation of \(f\) over a partition \(P\): the total length of the vertical steps between consecutive partition points.










Figure 15.2: Interactive: refining the partition (each refinement halves every interval) can only increase \(V(f,P)\), which climbs to \(TV(f)\).









ImportantTheorem 15.2 — \(f\) is of bounded variation iff



\(f\) is of bounded variation if and only if there exist increasing functions \(g,h\) so that \(f = g-h\)


There is a one-to-one correspondence between signed measures and right-continuous functions of bounded variation, which we discuss hereafter.






NoteDefinition 15.3 — Absolutely continuous function



\(f : [0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) is absolutely continuous if for all \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) so that if \(0 \leq x_1 < y_1 < x_2 < y_2 < \ldots < x_n < y_n \leq 1\) and \[\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - x_i) < \delta\], then \[\sum_{i=1}^n |f(y_i) - f(x_i)| < \epsilon\]








ImportantProposition 15.4 — Absolute continuity of a function



Let \(f\) be a nonnegative right-continuous increasing function on \([0,1]\) with \(f(0) = 0\). Then \(f\) is absolutely continuous if and only if \(\mu_f << m\) where \(m\) is the Lebesgue measure.


This is consistent with the result for Cantor ternary function (which is n.n. right continuous and increasing). The corresponding Cantor ternary measure (which again is a unique finite Borel measure) where \(\mu_C(C) = 1\) and \(m(C) = 0\) so clearly \(\mu_C\) is not absolutely continuous wrt to \(m\). By contrapositive, \(F_c\) is therefore not absolutely continuous.






ImportantProposition 15.5 — Absolute continuity implies bounded variation



If \(f:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb R\) is absolutely continuous, then it has bounded variation.



The fundamental theorem of calculus
If \(f:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb R\) is increasing, does \[\int_0^1 f'(x) dx = f(1) - f(0) ?\] Recall that an increasing function has a derivative a.e (Theorem 14.7).






CautionExample 15.6 — The FTC fails for the Cantor function



The Cantor ternary function \(F_C\) (Theorem 4.6) is increasing and continuous, with \(F_C(0) = 0\) and \(F_C(1) = 1\). By Corollary 4.7 (c), \(F_C' = 0\) almost everywhere: \(F_C\) is constant on each open interval removed in the construction of the Cantor set, and these intervals have total length \(1\). Hence \[\int_0^1 F_C'(x)\,dx = 0 < 1 = F_C(1) - F_C(0).\] So the answer to the question above is no in general: being increasing, and even continuous, is not enough, and the inequality in the next theorem can be strict. The missing ingredient is absolute continuity, see Theorem 15.8 (3): \(F_C\) is not absolutely continuous, since the Cantor measure \(\mu_C\) lives on the Cantor set, which has Lebesgue measure zero.








ImportantTheorem 15.7 — The fundamental theorem of calculus for monotone increasing functions



If \(f:[0,1]\rightarrow \mathbb R\) is monotone increasing, then \[\int_0^1 f'(x) dx \leq f(1) - f(0)\]








ImportantTheorem 15.8



Let \(f\) be a nonneg right-continuous monotone increasing function on \([0,1]\) with \(f(0) = 0\). Let \(\mu_f\) be the associated measure on \([0,1]\) and consider the Lebesgue decomposition \(\mu_f = \mu_s + \mu_{ac}\) with respect to Lebesgue measure. Then:

The Radon-Nikodym derivative of \(\mu_{ac}\) with respect to Lebesgue measure is given by \(f'\).
\(\mu_{ac}[0,1] = \int_0^1 f'(x)\, dx\).
\(f\) is absolutely continuous if and only if \(\int_0^1 f'(x)\, dx = f(1) - f(0)\). (So the second FTC holds if and only if \(f\) is absolutely continuous.)
\(\mu_f\) is singular if and only if \(f'(x) = 0\) a.e.









CautionExample 15.9 — A singular measure



By Theorem 15.8, we have that \(\mu_C\) is singular iff \(F'_C(x) = 0\) lebesgue a.e., which we know is true. So the Cantor measure is a singular measure.
